docs.title: Flan: Turbulent Trace Impurity Transport
docs.text: Welcome to Flan's documentation! The code is named after Shawn's dog, Flannery. It does not stand for anything. New users to the code see Getting Started for a high-level introduction to the code.

docs.title: Input Options
docs.text:
Input options are set in your input file through the inpts map, e.g.:

inpts["case_name"] = "my_case";
inpts["imp_num"] = 10000;
inpts["imp_mass_amu"] = 183.84;

Any option you don't set uses the default value listed below. The options are grouped by what they control.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text: Option Type Default Description case_name string "undefined" Name of the simulation case. The results are saved to <case_name>.nc. use_gpu string "off" Whether to run the simulation on GPUs. Valid values: "off", "cuda". seed int 4 Base seed for the random number generators. A negative value seeds them from the clock so each run is different. The MPI rank is added to the seed so each rank gets a different sequence. slot_cap int 1048576 Maximum number of particle slots, i.e., the most particles followed at once. The number of slots used is the smaller of this and imp_num. print_interval int 10 Number of progress updates printed while particles are followed. For example, 10 prints an update every 10% of particles.

docs.title: Background plasma
docs.text: Option Type Default Description bkg_source string "gkeyll" Source of the background plasma, either a built-in test background or a Gkeyll simulation. Valid values: "test", "gkeyll". min_ne float 1e15 Lower limit on the electron density (m^-3). min_te float 0.1 Lower limit on the electron temperature (eV). min_ti float 0.1 Lower limit on the ion temperature (eV), applied when calculating collisions with the background ions.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Option Type Default Description test_opt string "gyrate" Which built-in test case to run when using the test background. Valid values: "gyrate", "exb", "gradb", "polarization", "curvature", "friction_force". save_track string "off" Whether to save particle tracks to the output file. Valid values: "off", "on".

docs.title: Gkeyll
docs.text: Option Type Default Description gkyl_dir string "undefined" Directory containing the Gkeyll simulation files. gkyl_casename string "undefined" Name of the Gkeyll case, i.e., the prefix of its output files. gkyl_frame_start int 0 First Gkeyll frame to load. gkyl_frame_end int 1 Last Gkeyll frame to load. The range from gkyl_frame_start to gkyl_frame_end is inclusive. gkyl_elec_name string "elc" Name of the electron species in the Gkeyll simulation. gkyl_ion_name string "ion" Name of the main ion species in the Gkeyll simulation. gkyl_elec_mass_amu float 0.000548 Electron mass used in the Gkeyll simulation (amu). gkyl_ion_mass_amu float 2.014 Main ion mass used in the Gkeyll simulation (amu). gkyl_file_type string "binary" File format of the Gkeyll output. Valid values: "binary". gkyl_moment_type string "bimaxwellian" Type of moment files in the Gkeyll output. Collisions need "bimaxwellian", which provides the ion parallel flow and perpendicular velocity used to calculate the background flow. Valid values: "bimaxwellian", "maxwellian", "m0m1m2". calc_grad_elec string "off" Whether to calculate the electric field gradient. This is not implemented yet, so turning it on only prints a warning. Valid values: "off", "on".

docs.title: Geometry and boundaries
docs.text: Option Type Default Description tbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the start and end of the background time range. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic". min_xbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the minimum x boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". max_xbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the maximum x boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". min_ybound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the minimum y boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". max_ybound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the maximum y boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". min_zbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the minimum z boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". max_zbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the maximum z boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". lcfs_x float 0.0 x coordinate of the last closed flux surface. lcfs_y float 0.0 y coordinate of the last closed flux surface. lcfs_z float 0.0 z coordinate of the last closed flux surface. imp_xbound_buffer float 0.0 Buffer distance at the x boundaries. With an absorbing boundary, a particle is absorbed once it is within this distance of the boundary. imp_ybound_buffer float 0.0 Buffer distance at the y boundaries. With an absorbing boundary, a particle is absorbed once it is within this distance of the boundary. imp_zbound_buffer float 0.0 Buffer distance at the z boundaries. With an absorbing boundary, a particle is absorbed once it is within this distance of the boundary. sep_x_bc_xp_z1 float 0.0 First z value for the separatrix x boundary condition near the X-point. sep_x_bc_xp_z2 float 0.0 Second z value for the separatrix x boundary condition near the X-point.

docs.title: Impurity properties
docs.text: Option Type Default Description imp_atom_num int 74 Atomic number of the impurity. imp_mass_amu float 183.84 Mass of the impurity (amu). imp_init_charge int 1 Charge state the impurities start with.

docs.title: Impurity transport
docs.text: Option Type Default Description imp_num int 1 Total number of impurity particles to follow. imp_tstart_opt string "single_value" How each impurity's starting time is chosen: a single value (imp_tstart_val), uniformly between imp_trange_min and imp_trange_max, or uniformly over the full background time range. Valid values: "single_value", "range", "full_range". imp_tstart_val float 0.0 Starting time of every impurity when imp_tstart_opt is "single_value" (s). imp_trange_min float 0.0 Lower limit of the starting time range when imp_tstart_opt is "range" (s). imp_trange_max float 0.0 Upper limit of the starting time range when imp_tstart_opt is "range" (s). imp_xstart_opt string "single_value" How each impurity's starting x coordinate is chosen: a single value (imp_xstart_val), uniformly between imp_xrange_min and imp_xrange_max, or uniformly over the full x range of the background. Valid values: "single_value", "range", "full_range". imp_xstart_val float 0.0 Starting x coordinate of every impurity when imp_xstart_opt is "single_value". imp_xrange_min float 0.0 Lower limit of the starting x range when imp_xstart_opt is "range". imp_xrange_max float 0.0 Upper limit of the starting x range when imp_xstart_opt is "range". imp_ystart_opt string "single_value" How each impurity's starting y coordinate is chosen: a single value (imp_ystart_val), uniformly between imp_yrange_min and imp_yrange_max, or uniformly over the full y range of the background. Valid values: "single_value", "range", "full_range". imp_ystart_val float 0.0 Starting y coordinate of every impurity when imp_ystart_opt is "single_value". imp_yrange_min float 0.0 Lower limit of the starting y range when imp_ystart_opt is "range". imp_yrange_max float 0.0 Upper limit of the starting y range when imp_ystart_opt is "range". imp_zstart_opt string "single_value" How each impurity's starting z coordinate is chosen: a single value (imp_zstart_val), uniformly between imp_zrange_min and imp_zrange_max, or uniformly over the full z range of the background. Valid values: "single_value", "range", "full_range". imp_zstart_val float 0.0 Starting z coordinate of every impurity when imp_zstart_opt is "single_value". imp_zrange_min float 0.0 Lower limit of the starting z range when imp_zstart_opt is "range". imp_zrange_max float 0.0 Upper limit of the starting z range when imp_zstart_opt is "range". imp_temp_start_opt string "main_ion" How each impurity's starting temperature is chosen: a single value (imp_temp_start_val) or the local main ion temperature. Starting velocities are sampled from an isotropic Maxwellian at this temperature. Valid values: "single_value", "main_ion". imp_temp_start_val float 0.0 Starting temperature of every impurity when imp_temp_start_opt is "single_value" (eV). imp_collisions string "nanbu" Collision model for the impurities, either off or the Nanbu model. Valid values: "off", "nanbu". imp_time_step_opt string "constant" Whether the impurity time step is constant or variable. Valid values: "constant", "variable". imp_time_step float 1e-8 Impurity time step (s). imp_time_step_min float 1e-12 Minimum impurity time step when the time step is variable (s). imp_source_scale_fact float 1.0 Impurity source scaling factor (particles/s), i.e., how many real particles a single simulated particle represents. Used to convert the Monte Carlo counts into a density. imp_iz_recomb string "on" Whether impurity ionization and recombination are on. Valid values: "off", "on". imp_max_time float 1e10 Maximum time a particle is followed for (s). A particle that exceeds it is killed and counted in a warning at the end of the run.

docs.title: Variance reduction (temporarily removed)
docs.text: Option Type Default Description var_red_split string "off" When particles are split for variance reduction: never, at ionization/recombination events, or at collisions. Valid values: "off", "iz_rec", "coll". var_red_import string "median" Method used to calculate particle importance for variance reduction. Valid values: "median", "exp_dist", "exp_time". var_red_freq float 0.1 How often variance reduction is applied. var_red_min_weight float 0.1 Minimum particle weight for variance reduction. var_red_med_mod float 1.0 Modifier applied to the median importance for variance reduction. var_red_rusrol string "off" Whether to use Russian roulette for variance reduction. Valid values: "off", "on". var_red_rusrol_prob float 0.5 Probability used for Russian roulette.

docs.title: OpenADAS
docs.text: Option Type Default Description openadas_root string "undefined" Directory containing the OpenADAS rate coefficient files. openadas_year int 50 Year of the OpenADAS data files to use.

docs.title: Journal Articles
docs.text:
• S. A. Zamperini, T. N. Bernard, S. Andersen, A. C. D. Hoffmann, D. L. Rudakov, and T. Abrams, "Fully generalized, turbulent trace impurity transport with Gkeyll and Flan in the DIII-D far-SOL," Plasma Physics and Controlled Fusion 68, 075013 (2026). doi:10.1088/1361-6587/ae836b

    The first official Flan publication. Validation tests are shown, and tungsten transport in the DIII-D far-SOL is simulated. Main takeaways are an early attempt at extracting the anomalous diffusion and pinch velocities as well as the observation that transport away from the wall increases with atomic number.

  • S. A. Zamperini, T. N. Bernard, D. L. Rudakov, and J. A. Boedo, "Turbulent drifts of impurity ions as an explanation for anomalous radial transport in the far-SOL of DIII-D," Nuclear Fusion 64, 074002 (2024). doi:10.1088/1741-4326/ad4c78

    A python-based precursor to Flan that tracked impurities via their guiding centers. It became clear that the guiding center approximation was violated because the fluctuations were on the same scale as the tungsten gyroradius, and that the full gyro-orbit needed to be resolved. This was the key issue that showed the need for a proper high-performance code that resolved the gyro-orbit and all the additional Monte Carlo structure.

docs.title: Linux Installation
docs.text: Installing Flan on a general Linux machine involves downloading and compiling the dependencies and then compiling the code via CMake.

docs.title: Install Dependencies
docs.text:
Navigate to the top-level flan/ directory and run:

machines/mkdeps.linux.sh

This will download and install all the dependencies in $HOME/flansoft by default. If you wish to have them installed elsewhere, change the following line in mkdeps.linux.sh to the desired directory:

export FLANSOFT=/path/to/dir/flansoft

This script also handles creating the conda environment that Flan must run in. You must activate the environment before running Flan with conda activate flan.

docs.title: Install Flan
docs.text:
Navigate to flan/build. This is where Flan will be compiled as a library. Run CMake to create the Makefile, then make and install the library.

cd build
cmake ..
make && make install

Flan will be installed at flan/lib/libflan.so. This also creates a bash script scripts/flan_setup.sh, which is used when setting up a new case.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: There are probably numerous issues that can pop up, as each machine is different. Please reach out to a developer if you encounter issues so the instructions can be updated.

docs.title: Perlmutter Installation
docs.text: Installing Flan on Perlmutter involves downloading and compiling the dependencies and then compiling the code via CMake. It uses the NERSC provided Cray C/C++ compiler wrappers (cc/CC).

docs.title: Install Dependencies
docs.text:
Navigate to the top-level flan/ directory and run:

machines/mkdeps.perlmutter.sh

This will download and install all the dependencies in $HOME/flansoft by default. If you wish to have them installed elsewhere, change the following line in mkdeps.perlmutter.sh to the desired directory:

export FLANSOFT=/path/to/dir/flansoft

This script also handles creating the conda environment that Flan must run in. You must activate the environment before running Flan by first loading the conda module with module load conda and then activating the environment with conda activate flan.

docs.title: Install Flan
docs.text:
Navigate to flan/build. This is where Flan will be compiled as a library. Run CMake to create the Makefile, then make and install the library. On Perlmutter you should enable CUDA.

cd build
cmake .. -DENABLE_CUDA=ON
make && make install

Flan will be installed at flan/lib/libflan.so.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Please reach out to a developer if you encounter issues so the instructions can be updated.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Flan is built as a modern C++23 project using CMake and supports both serial and hybrid MPI/OpenMP execution. This page walks you through installing and building Flan on laptops, workstations, and HPC systems such as Perlmutter.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Flan has the following dependencies:

  • C++23-capable compiler
  • CMake ≥ 3.26
  • OpenMP support
  • MPI
  • MPICH, OpenMPI, Cray-MPICH, etc.
  • HDF5
  • NetCDF
  • zlib
  • conda (or mamba)

HDF5, NetCDF and zlib are installed by machine-specific scripts to install dependencies, found in machines/. Other dependencies must be provided by the computing environment.

docs.title: Clone the Repository
docs.text:
Cloning the repository is straightforward. This will clone it into flan/:

git clone https://github.com/shawnzamperini/flan.git

docs.title: Machine specific instructions
docs.text:
Select your machine from the following list. Use Linux for a general purpose installation, e.g., a personal laptop.

  • Linux
  • Perlmutter

docs.title: Collisions
docs.text: Impurity ions in Flan undergo Coulomb collisions with the background ions and electrons through the Nanbu collision model. Collisions are turned on with imp_collisions = "nanbu", and are applied once per time step, just before the Boris push (see Impurity Transport).

docs.title: The Nanbu model
docs.text:
The Nanbu model was introduced in:

K. Nanbu, "Theory of cumulative small-angle collisions in plasmas," Phys. Rev. E 55, 4642–4652 (1997). doi:10.1103/PhysRevE.55.4642

A charged particle moving through a plasma undergoes a huge number of small-angle Coulomb collisions. Following each one is out of the question, and Nanbu's insight was that their cumulative effect over a time step \(\Delta t\) can be replaced by a single deflection of the relative velocity by an angle \(\chi\). The distribution of \(\chi\) depends only on one dimensionless parameter,

\[ s = \frac{\ln\Lambda}{4\pi}\left(\frac{q_a q_b}{\varepsilon_0 \mu_{ab}}\right)^2 \frac{n_b}{g^3}\,\Delta t, \]

where \(q_a\) and \(q_b\) are the charges of the impurity and the background species, \(\mu_{ab}\) is their reduced mass, \(n_b\) is the background density, \(g\) is the magnitude of their relative velocity and \(\ln\Lambda\) is the Coulomb logarithm. \(s\) is roughly the number of collision times that fit in \(\Delta t\), so it measures how collisional the step is:

  • \(s \ll 1\): the step is weakly collisional, and \(\chi\) is small.
  • \(s \gg 1\): the particle has "forgotten" its initial direction, and \(\chi\) is isotropic.

The model covers the whole range of \(s\) in one distribution, which is its main strength. A Monte Carlo collision step built on it goes smoothly from weak, small-angle scattering to full isotropization without changing algorithms.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: The model lives in the Collisions namespace (src/collisions.cpp, and src/cuda/collisions.cu for the GPU). Every alive, charged particle collides first with the background ions and then with the background electrons (the friction_force test case skips electron collisions). For each species, the steps are as follows.

docs.title: 1. Sample a background particle
docs.text:
The local \(n_e\), \(T_e\), \(T_i\) and flow velocity \(\mathbf{u}\) are interpolated to the particle's position and time. Each Cartesian component of a background particle's velocity is then sampled from a drifting Maxwellian:

\[ v_{b,j} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(u_j,\ \sqrt{T_b/m_b}\right), \]

and the relative velocity is \(\mathbf{g} = \mathbf{v}_a - \mathbf{v}_b\). The same flow velocity, from the Gkeyll ion moments, is used for both ions and electrons. The background masses come from gkyl_ion_mass_amu and gkyl_elec_mass_amu.

docs.title: 2. Calculate s
docs.text:
\(s\) is calculated with the formula above, with an impurity of charge state \(Z\) (\(q_a = Ze\)) and a singly charged background (\(q_b = e\), \(n_b = n_e\)). The instantaneous \(g\) of the sampled pair is used in \(g^3\).

The Coulomb logarithm is \(\ln\Lambda = \ln(\lambda_D / b_0)\). \(\lambda_D\) is the electron Debye length, and \(b_0\) is the impact parameter for 90° scattering evaluated at the expected value of the relative velocity, \(\langle g^2\rangle = 3T_b/\mu_{ab}\):

\[ b_0 = \frac{q_a q_b}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\,\mu_{ab}\,\langle g^2 \rangle}. \]

docs.title: 3. Calculate A
docs.text:
The shape of the \(\chi\) distribution is set by \(A(s)\), the solution of

\[ \coth A - \frac{1}{A} = e^{-s}. \]

There is no closed form for \(A\), so it is linearly interpolated from a table (include/nanbu_s_a.h, generated by python/calc_nanbu_A.py) for \(0.01 \le s \le 5\). Outside this range, the asymptotic limits are used: \(A = 1/s\) for \(s < 0.01\) and \(A = 3e^{-s}\) for \(s > 5\).

docs.title: 4. Sample the deflection angle
docs.text:
With a uniform random number \(U \in (0, 1]\), the deflection angle is sampled by inverting the cumulative distribution:

\[ \cos\chi = \frac{1}{A}\ln\!\left(e^{-A} + 2U\sinh A\right). \]

For \(s < 0.02\), the small-\(s\) limit \(\cos\chi = 1 + s\ln U\) is used, and for \(s > 6\) the deflection is isotropic, \(\cos\chi = 2U - 1\).

docs.title: 5. Update the velocity
docs.text:
\(\mathbf{g}\) is rotated by \(\chi\) about a random azimuthal angle \(\varepsilon \in [0, 2\pi)\), and the impurity velocity becomes

\[ \mathbf{v}_a' = \mathbf{v}_a - \frac{m_b}{m_a + m_b} \left[\mathbf{g}\,(1 - \cos\chi) + \mathbf{h}\sin\chi\right], \]

where \(\mathbf{h}\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{g}\), has the same magnitude, and points in the direction set by \(\varepsilon\). Only the impurity is updated. The background is fixed, so this is a test-particle model.

docs.title: Neutrals
docs.text: Neutrals (\(Z = 0\)) are skipped, since they don't undergo Coulomb collisions. Neutral–plasma interactions such as charge exchange or elastic scattering off background neutrals are not included in Flan.

docs.title: Safeguards
docs.text:
A few limits keep the calculation well behaved in extreme corners of the background:

Quantity Limit \(n_e\), \(T_e\), \(T_i\) At least min_ne, min_te and min_ti \(\ln\Lambda\) At least 1 \(g\) At least \(10^{-3}\) m/s, to avoid dividing by zero in \(s\) \(\cos\chi\) Clamped to \([-1, 1]\), to guard against rounding errors

docs.title: When the model is valid
docs.text:
The Nanbu model rests on a few assumptions. Each one is satisfied in typical edge and scrape-off layer plasmas, but each can break down.

Valid when:

  • The plasma is weakly coupled, \(\ln\Lambda \gg 1\). The model assumes that the deflection is dominated by many distant, small-angle collisions, the same assumption behind the Landau/Fokker–Planck collision operator. Typical edge plasmas have \(\ln\Lambda \approx 10\)–\(15\), which is well within this regime.
  • The impurities are trace. The background is treated as a fixed Maxwellian that the impurities don't modify, so momentum and energy given to the background are not fed back into it. This is fine as long as the impurity density is small compared to the plasma density.
  • The background is close to a Maxwellian. Background velocities are sampled from a drifting, isotropic Maxwellian with a single temperature, so temperature anisotropy and non-Maxwellian tails are not captured.
  • The background changes little over one time step. The plasma parameters are evaluated once at the start of the step and held fixed for the collision.

One thing the model does not require is a time step much smaller than the collision time. The \(\chi\) distribution is valid for any \(s\), which is the point of the model. In practice, Flan's time step is set by resolving the gyromotion in the Boris push, which usually makes \(s\) small anyway.

Invalid or questionable when:

  • \(\ln\Lambda\) approaches a few or less. This happens in very cold, dense plasmas, e.g., deeply detached divertor conditions. Large-angle collisions become important, and the small-angle picture is no longer accurate. If \(\ln\Lambda\) falls below 1 it's clamped to 1, so results in these regions should be treated with caution.
  • The impurity concentration is high. The impurities would noticeably change the background (and \(n_i \ne n_e\)), which the test-particle approach can't capture.
  • The background has more than one ion species, or the main ions aren't singly charged. \(q_b = e\) and \(n_b = n_e\) are assumed for the ion collisions, so collisions with other ion species, e.g., impurity–impurity collisions, are not included.
  • Neutral collisions matter. As noted above, only Coulomb collisions with charged background species are modeled.

docs.title: Impurity Transport
docs.text: Flan follows impurity ions through a background plasma (usually from Gkeyll) by integrating each particle's full orbit, including its gyromotion. No guiding-center approximation is made. Each particle is pushed through the background electric and magnetic fields with the Boris algorithm, and its charge state and velocity are updated between pushes by ionization/recombination and Coulomb collisions.

docs.title: The main loop
docs.text:
Particles are held in a fixed number of slots. Each pass through the main loop (ImpurityTransport namespace, impurity_transport.cpp) advances every alive particle in the slots by one time step, imp_time_step:

  1. Ionization/recombination (if imp_iz_recomb = "on"): the charge state may change based on OpenADAS rate coefficients. See Ionization/Recombination.
  2. Collisions (if imp_collisions = "nanbu"): the velocity is scattered by the background ions and electrons with the Nanbu model. See Collisions.
  3. Boris push: the velocity is updated from the Lorentz force (described below).
  4. Step: the position is moved forward by \(\mathbf{v}\,\Delta t\), and the particle's time is advanced.
  5. Bounds check: particles that leave the domain are absorbed, wrapped (periodic boundaries) or otherwise handled by the boundary conditions.
  6. Fill slots: the slots of dead particles are filled with newly launched particles until none are left to follow.
  7. Find cell: the grid cell and background time frame that contain each particle are found.
  8. Record statistics: each particle's contribution to the impurity density and other outputs is added to the cell it's in.

The loop runs until every slot is dead and there are no particles left to launch. A particle is also killed once it has been followed for longer than imp_max_time.

Each step has a CPU (OpenMP) and GPU (CUDA) implementation. A wrapper function picks between them based on use_gpu, so the physics is the same either way.

docs.title: Coordinates
docs.text:
The background is defined on a computational grid \((x, y, z)\) that is generally curvilinear, e.g., field-aligned coordinates. The Lorentz force is much simpler to evaluate in Cartesian space, though, so each particle carries two velocities:

  • \((v_X, v_Y, v_Z)\): the Cartesian velocity. This is what the Boris algorithm updates.
  • \((v_x, v_y, v_z)\): the velocity in computational coordinates. This is what moves the particle on the grid.

After the Cartesian velocity has been updated, the computational velocity is found with the reciprocal (contravariant) basis vectors \( abla x\), \( abla y\), \( abla z\):

\[ v_x = rac{\partial x}{\partial X} v_X + rac{\partial x}{\partial Y} v_Y + rac{\partial x}{\partial Z} v_Z \]

and similarly for \(v_y\) and \(v_z\). The basis vectors are stored at the cell centers, and are trilinearly interpolated to the particle's position.

docs.title: The Boris algorithm
docs.text: The Boris algorithm is the standard method for pushing charged particles through electric and magnetic fields. It is second-order accurate and time-reversible. A pure magnetic field does no work, and the algorithm conserves energy exactly in that case, so the gyro-orbit doesn't drift over the many gyro-periods a particle is followed for.

docs.title: Leapfrog staggering
docs.text:
Positions and velocities are staggered by half a time step (leapfrog):

\[ \mathbf{x}_n = \mathbf{x}(t_n), \qquad \mathbf{v}_n = \mathbf{v}(t_n - \Delta t/2) \]

Particles are launched with the position and velocity at the same time, so the velocity is pushed backwards by half a time step (\(-\Delta t/2\)) before the main loop starts. This sets up the staggering.

docs.title: Field interpolation
docs.text:
Before the push, \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are found at the particle's position and time:

  1. Each Cartesian component, and the magnitude, is trilinearly interpolated in space between the centers of the cell containing the particle and its neighbors on the particle's side. This is done for the particle's background time frame and the next one (the previous one if the particle is in the last frame).
  2. The two values are linearly interpolated in time to the particle's time.
  3. The interpolated vector is rescaled to the interpolated magnitude.

Interpolation keeps the fields continuous as a particle crosses cell boundaries and background time frames. With piecewise-constant fields, particles get unphysical "kicks" at every boundary and drift off the field line (numerical diffusion). Interpolating in time also matters for time-dependent drifts like the polarization drift.

The rescaling in step 3 is a deliberate trade-off. An interpolated vector is almost always shorter than the true field, which would make the gyroradius wrong. Rescaling to the interpolated magnitude gets the gyro-orbit right, at the cost of a small discontinuity at cell boundaries. A particle spends far more time inside a cell than crossing a boundary, so getting the orbit right matters more.

docs.title: The push
docs.text:
With the charge-to-mass ratio \(q/m\) (where \(q = Z e\) for charge state \(Z\)), the velocity is advanced from \(\mathbf{v}_n\) to \(\mathbf{v}_{n+1}\):

  1. Half electric kick:

    \[ \mathbf{v}^- = \mathbf{v}_n + \frac{q}{m}\mathbf{E}\,\frac{\Delta t}{2} \]

  2. Magnetic rotation. With

    \[ \mathbf{t} = \frac{q}{m}\mathbf{B}\,\frac{\Delta t}{2}, \qquad \mathbf{s} = \frac{2\mathbf{t}}{1 + |\mathbf{t}|^2} \]

    the velocity is rotated about \(\mathbf{B}\) in two steps:

    \[ \mathbf{v}' = \mathbf{v}^- + \mathbf{v}^- \times \mathbf{t}, \qquad \mathbf{v}^+ = \mathbf{v}^- + \mathbf{v}' \times \mathbf{s} \]

  3. Second half electric kick:

    \[ \mathbf{v}_{n+1} = \mathbf{v}^+ + \frac{q}{m}\mathbf{E}\,\frac{\Delta t}{2} \]

The rotation leaves \(|\mathbf{v}^+| = |\mathbf{v}^-|\), so all energy change comes from the electric field. Finally, \((v_x, v_y, v_z)\) are calculated from the new Cartesian velocity (see Coordinates), and the step moves the particle:

\[ \mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n + \mathbf{v}_{n+1}\,\Delta t \]

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The CPU version is Boris::update_velocity_cpu in src/boris.cpp, parallelized over particles with OpenMP. The GPU version is update_velocity_kernel in src/cuda/boris.cu, with one thread per particle. The two use the same push. The GPU version builds the interpolation stencils with the helpers in src/cuda/interpolate.cu. The core of the push is:

// Charge state times the (positive) elementary charge, divided by mass
double q_m {slots.q()[i] * -Constants::charge_e / slots.mass()};

// t vector
for (int j {}; j < 3; ++j) t[j] = q_m * B_local[j] * 0.5 * dt;
double tmag2 {t[0]*t[0] + t[1]*t[1] + t[2]*t[2]};

// s vector
for (int j {}; j < 3; ++j) s[j] = 2 * t[j] / (1.0 + tmag2);

// Half electric kick
for (int j {}; j < 3; ++j) vminus[j] = v[j] + q_m * E_local[j] * 0.5 * dt;

// Magnetic rotation
vminus_cross_t = Utilities::cross_product(vminus, t);
for (int j {}; j < 3; ++j) vprime[j] = vminus[j] + vminus_cross_t[j];
vprime_cross_s = Utilities::cross_product(vprime, s);
for (int j {}; j < 3; ++j) vplus[j] = vminus[j] + vprime_cross_s[j];

// Second half electric kick
slots.set_vX(i, vplus[0] + q_m * E_local[0] * 0.5 * dt);
slots.set_vY(i, vplus[1] + q_m * E_local[1] * 0.5 * dt);
slots.set_vZ(i, vplus[2] + q_m * E_local[2] * 0.5 * dt);

Constants::charge_e is the electron charge (\(-1.602\times10^{-19}\) C), so q * -charge_e is the positive ion charge \(Ze\).

docs.title: Neutrals
docs.text:
Neutrals are handled correctly

Particles in charge state \(Z = 0\) are followed in the same loop as the ions and need no special treatment in the Boris push. With \(q = 0\):

  • \(q/m = 0\), so both electric kicks vanish,
  • \(\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{s} = 0\), so there is no magnetic rotation,

and \(\mathbf{v}_{n+1} = \mathbf{v}_n\). A neutral moves in a straight line at constant velocity, as it should, and it isn't affected by the fields.

The other steps also treat neutrals correctly:

  • Collisions: neutrals are skipped, since they don't undergo Coulomb collisions.
  • Ionization/recombination: a neutral can ionize to \(Z = 1\) but can't recombine, so its recombination probability is zero. Once it's ionized, the next Boris push uses the new charge, and the particle starts to gyrate.

A neutral's velocity can only change when it ionizes. Until then, it just streams through the plasma.

docs.title: Ionization and Recombination
docs.text: As an impurity moves through the plasma, its charge state changes through electron-impact ionization and recombination. Flan models both as random events whose probabilities come from OpenADAS rate coefficients. They are turned on with imp_iz_recomb = "on", and are applied once per time step, at the start of each pass through the main loop (see Impurity Transport).

docs.title: Rate coefficients
docs.text:
The rate coefficients come from the OpenADAS database (open.adas.ac.uk), in ADF11 format:

  • SCD files: effective ionization rate coefficients, \(S_Z(n_e, T_e)\), for \(Z \to Z+1\).
  • ACD files: effective recombination rate coefficients, \(\alpha_{Z}(n_e, T_e)\), for \(Z \to Z-1\).

These are effective (collisional-radiative) coefficients. They depend on both \(n_e\) and \(T_e\), and they include the effect of the excited-state populations. Recombination includes radiative, dielectronic and three-body recombination.

Each file is read from

[openadas_root]/scd[openadas_year]/scd[openadas_year]_[element].dat
[openadas_root]/acd[openadas_year]/acd[openadas_year]_[element].dat

where openadas_root and openadas_year are input options (openadas_year defaults to 50) and the element is chosen with imp_atom_num. For example, tungsten with the default year reads scd50/scd50_w.dat and acd50/acd50_w.dat. The supported elements are H through Ne, Al, Si, Cl, Ar, Fe, Kr, Mo, Xe and W.

The files store \(\log_{10}\) of the densities (cm\(^{-3}\)), temperatures (eV) and rate coefficients (cm\(^3\)/s). These are converted to m\(^{-3}\), eV and m\(^3\)/s when they are read in (OpenADAS::read_rate_coefficients in src/openadas.cpp).

docs.title: Interpolation
docs.text:
For each particle, \(n_e\) and \(T_e\) are interpolated to the particle's position and time, the same way as in the Boris push. The rate coefficient for the particle's charge state is then bilinearly interpolated in \((T_e, n_e)\) from the table.

If \(n_e\) or \(T_e\) fall outside the range of the OpenADAS data, they are clamped to the nearest edge of the table. The rates are never extrapolated.

docs.title: Charge-state update
docs.text:
During one time step \(\Delta t\), a particle in charge state \(Z\) ionizes with probability

\[ P_\text{iz} = S_Z(n_e, T_e)\, n_e\, \Delta t \]

and recombines with probability

\[ P_\text{rec} = \alpha_Z(n_e, T_e)\, n_e\, \Delta t. \]

Two uniform random numbers \(U_1, U_2 \in [0, 1)\) are drawn, and the charge becomes

\[ Z \to Z + [U_1 < P_\text{iz}] - [U_2 < P_\text{rec}], \]

where \([\cdot]\) is 1 if the condition is true and 0 otherwise. If both events happen in the same step they cancel and the charge state is unchanged, so the charge changes by at most one per step.

A fully stripped ion (\(Z\) equal to the atomic number) can't ionize, so \(P_\text{iz} = 0\). The velocity is not changed by an ionization or recombination event. The new charge simply takes effect in the next Boris push and collision step.

The CPU version is OpenADAS::ioniz_recomb (src/openadas.cpp), and the GPU version is ioniz_recomb_kernel (src/cuda/openadas.cu).

docs.title: Neutrals
docs.text:
Neutrals are handled correctly

A neutral (\(Z = 0\)) can ionize to \(Z = 1\) using the \(Z = 0 \to 1\) SCD coefficient, but it can't recombine, so \(P_\text{rec} = 0\). Once it's ionized, it is pushed by the fields and starts to undergo collisions. See Impurity Transport and Collisions.

docs.title: Choosing the time step
docs.text:
\(P = R\, n_e\, \Delta t\) is the first-order expansion of the exact probability \(1 - e^{-R\, n_e\, \Delta t}\), and it's only accurate when \(P \ll 1\). The update also allows at most one ionization or recombination per step. Both mean the time step must be short compared to the ionization and recombination times, \(1/(S_Z n_e)\) and \(1/(\alpha_Z n_e)\).

If \(P > 1\), the event always happens and the true rate is underestimated. Flan counts how often this happens, and prints a warning at the end of the run:

Warning: Ionization probability was > 1.0 for N particles. Consider using a smaller time step.

(and similarly for recombination). The counter is incremented each time step that the probability is above 1, so \(N\) counts particle-steps rather than unique particles. If these warnings show up for more than a handful of particle-steps, reduce imp_time_step. This is most likely for low charge states in hot, dense plasma, where ionization is fastest.

docs.title: When the model is valid
docs.text:
Valid when:

  • The time step resolves the atomic time scales, i.e., \(P \ll 1\) (see above).
  • The plasma is within the range of the OpenADAS tables. Outside the table, the edge values are used, which can be a poor approximation, e.g., at temperatures far below the lowest tabulated \(T_e\).
  • The electrons are close to Maxwellian. The ADAS coefficients are averaged over a Maxwellian electron distribution at \(T_e\).
  • The excited states are in quasi-steady state. The effective coefficients assume that excited-state populations relax much faster than the plasma conditions change along the impurity's path. This usually holds, though long-lived metastable states can violate it.

Not included:

  • Charge-exchange recombination with background neutrals, e.g., \(W^{Z+} + D^0 \to W^{(Z-1)+} + D^+\), which can be important in regions with a high neutral density.
  • Ionization by ions or photons. Only electron-impact ionization is included.
  • More than one charge change per step. See Choosing the time step.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Setting up a Flan case from scratch consists of the following steps:

  • Create case directory: flan_setup.sh
  • Modify input file
  • Compile input file with Flan
  • Run case/submit job

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
A built-in test case that demonstrates the ExB drift with a single particle will be used to show how to run Flan. First create the run directory with the command:

/path/to/flan/scripts/flan_setup.sh test_exb

This will create a directory called test_exb and populate it with an empty input file as well as the needed files to compile it with Flan. We will not cover the various input options here, and will instead copy over the input file used to run the ExB drift test:

cd test_exb
cp /path/to/flan/tests/test_exb.cpp .

The input file must have the same name as the directory because it is baked into the Makefile that was generated to compile the input file. Flan must be run in the conda environment that was created as part of the installation process because it contains some needed paths, primarily for interfacing with Gkeyll data. Ensure it's activated with conda activate flan. You typically will see (flan) at the start of your command line when it's activated. Next make the input file with just make.

Running the simulation depends on if you can run it from the command line or need to use a job scheduler. Running from the command line will be covered first, and job submission scripts will be provided after.

docs.title: Running from Command Line
docs.text:
To run from the command line simply run the executable:

./test_exb

By default, this will run with one MPI process and likely the maximum number of OpenMP threads available. On smaller machines like laptops or workstations only one MPI processes is needed since it is mainly for distributed computing across multiple compute nodes, such as on clusters. To explicitly set the number of OpenMP threads used by Flan, e.g., to 5, use:

OMP_NUM_THREADS=5 ./test_exb

You may often need to reduce the number of OpenMP threads to stay within memory limits of your machine, as each thread comes with memory overhead.

To control the number of MPI processes, e.g., to use 2, use:

mpiexec -np 2 ./test_exb

Alternative commands include mpirun and srun, depending on your system.

Control the number of OpenMP threads available to each process the same as before:

OMP_NUM_THREADS=5 mpiexec -np 2 ./test_exb

docs.title: Running with Job Submission Script
docs.text:
For convenience job submission scripts are provided for the following machines:

  • Perlmutter
  • Omega

docs.title: Running on Omega
docs.text: This page is under construction.

docs.title: Perlmutter Batch Script
docs.text:
The following is an example batch script used to submit a Flan job on Perlmutter. 

#!/bin/bash -l
#SBATCH --job-name=my-job-name
#SBATCH --account=m3739     # Update with project number
#SBATCH --nodes=2           # 2 nodes
#SBATCH --ntasks=2          # 2 MPI tasks
#SBATCH --constraint=cpu
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=128 # Use all CPUs on node
#SBATCH --qos=regular       # debug (only one node allowed) or regular
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00     # Run for an hour

# OpenMP settings
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK      # Match --cpus-per-task above
export OMP_PLACES=cores         # Bind threads to cores
export OMP_PROC_BIND=spread     # Spread threads across cores

# This controls the number of threads available in python. Make it match
# cpus-per-task
export NUMEXPR_MAX_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK

# Initialize conda for compute node
module load conda
conda activate flan

# Run Flan run
srun --cpu-bind=cores ./my_flan_case
Compile the input file as normal, using the Makefile provided when setting up a case directory. If the batch script is saved as submit-flan-perlmutter.sh, then submit the job with:

sbatch submit-flan-perlmutter.sh

Output is put into a generically named slurm file.

docs.title: function broadcast
docs.text:
void Background::Background::broadcast (
    MPI_Comm comm
)

Broadcasts the background from rank 0 to every other MPI rank.

Every rank must call this. After it returns, every rank holds a copy of the dimensions, the times and computational grid, the geometry data and the plasma and field data loaded on rank 0. Not broadcast are the time and grid min/max values, bR, the covariant magnetic field components (b_x, b_y, b_z) and the electric field gradient (gradeX, gradeY, gradeZ).

Parameters:

  • comm MPI communicator to broadcast over.

docs.title: function check_dim
docs.text:
bool Background::Background::check_dim (
    const int m_dim,
    const int in_dim,
    const std::string_view data,
    const int dim_num
)

Checks that a new dimension matches the dimension already stored.

A stored dimension of 0 means it has not been set yet, so any new dimension is accepted. Otherwise the two must be equal. A mismatch means the data is not being read in correctly or is from different Gkeyll runs, and an error message with both values is printed.

Parameters:

  • m_dim Dimension currently stored in the Background.
  • in_dim Dimension of the data being loaded.
  • data Name of the data being loaded (for the error message).
  • dim_num Which dimension (1-4) is being checked (for the error message).

Returns:

True if the dimensions are consistent, false otherwise.

docs.title: function interp_4d
docs.text:
BkgFPType Background::Background::interp_4d (
    const Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & vec4d,
    const double t0,
    const double x0,
    const double y0,
    const double z0
) const

Interpolates 4D background data at a given time and position.

This is a convenience wrapper around Utilities::interp_vec4d that passes in the background times and the x, y and z cell centers, so callers only need to supply the data and the point to evaluate it at.

Parameters:

  • vec4d Data to interpolate, stored as a function of (t, x, y, z).
  • t0 Time at which to evaluate the data.
  • x0 x-coordinate at which to evaluate the data.
  • y0 y-coordinate at which to evaluate the data.
  • z0 z-coordinate at which to evaluate the data.

Returns:

Interpolated value at (t0, x0, y0, z0).

docs.title: function set_dims
docs.text:
template<typename T>
void Background::Background::set_dims (
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & v,
    const std::string_view data
)

Checks the dimensions of a Vector4D against the stored dimensions and stores them if they are consistent.

Each of the four dimensions of v is checked with check_dim. If all four are consistent, they become the stored dimensions. If any are not, an error message is printed and the stored dimensions are left unchanged. The program is not stopped.

Template parameters:

  • T Data type stored in the Vector4D.

Parameters:

  • v Vector4D whose dimensions are checked.
  • data Name of the data being loaded (for the error message).

docs.title: function interp_recp
docs.text:
std::array< double, 9 > Boris::interp_recp (
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const int xidx,
    const int yidx,
    const int zidx,
    const double x,
    const double y,
    const double z
)

Interpolates the reciprocal (contravariant) basis vectors at the particle location.

These convert a Cartesian vector into its computational components, e.g., vx = dxdX * vX + dxdY * vY + dxdZ * vZ.

Each of the nine components is trilinearly interpolated between the centers of the cell containing the particle and its neighboring cells on the side of the particle, since that is where the basis vectors are defined.

Parameters:

  • bkg Background plasma holding the basis vectors.
  • xidx x index of the grid cell containing the particle.
  • yidx y index of the grid cell containing the particle.
  • zidx z index of the grid cell containing the particle.
  • x Computational x coordinate of the particle.
  • y Computational y coordinate of the particle.
  • z Computational z coordinate of the particle.

Returns:

Interpolated components in the order dxdX, dxdY, dxdZ, dydX, dydY, dydZ, dzdX, dzdY, dzdZ.

docs.title: function update_velocity_cpu
docs.text:
void Boris::update_velocity_cpu (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    const double dt
)

Advances the velocity of every particle by one time step using the Boris algorithm.

The electric and magnetic fields (components and magnitudes) are trilinearly interpolated in space to the particle location, at the particle's time frame and a neighboring one, and then linearly interpolated in time. This keeps the fields continuous at cell boundaries and between time frames, which avoids numerical diffusion and unphysical kicks. Each interpolated vector is then rescaled to the interpolated magnitude so the gyro-orbit is the correct size.

The standard Boris rotation then updates the Cartesian velocity (vX, vY, vZ). Velocities are stored at the half time steps before the position, i.e., x_i = x(t_i) and v_i = v(t_i - dt/2). Finally, the velocity in computational coordinates (vx, vy, vz) is calculated with the interpolated reciprocal basis vectors from interp_recp.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots. The velocities are updated in place.
  • bkg Background plasma holding the fields and basis vectors.
  • opts Simulation options. Currently unused.
  • dt Time step (s).

docs.title: function nanbu_calc_A
docs.text:
double Collisions::nanbu_calc_A (
    const double s
)

Calculates the A term in the Nanbu collision model (Eq. 13), which sets the shape of the distribution the deflection angle is sampled from.

For s < 0.01 (weakly collisional) A = 1 / s, and for s > 5 (strongly collisional) A = 3 exp(-s). In between, A is linearly interpolated from the precomputed table in nanbu_s_a.h, which was calculated using python/calc_nanbu.py.

Parameters:

  • s The s term from nanbu_calc_s.

Returns:

The A term.

docs.title: function nanbu_calc_chi
docs.text:
double Collisions::nanbu_calc_chi (
    const double s,
    const double A,
    pcg32 & rng
)

Samples the deflection angle chi in the Nanbu collision model (Eq. 17).

cos(chi) is found by directly inverting the cumulative distribution built from A, using a uniform random number U. For s < 0.02 the small-s limit 1 + s ln(U) is used, and for s > 6 the deflection is isotropic, 2U - 1. cos(chi) is clamped to [-1, 1] to guard against rounding errors.

Parameters:

  • s The s term from nanbu_calc_s.
  • A The A term from nanbu_calc_A.
  • rng Random number generator for this thread.

Returns:

Deflection angle chi (radians).

std::tuple< double, double, double, double > Collisions::nanbu_calc_s (
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const double imp_time_step,
    const double T,
    const double mass_kg,
    const double Te,
    const double ne,
    const double t,
    const double x,

    const double z,
    const double vX,
    const double vY,
    const double vZ,
    const int q,
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    pcg32 & rng
)

Calculates the s term in the Nanbu collision model (Eq. 19), which measures how collisional this time step is.

The relative velocity g is between the impurity and a background particle whose velocity is sampled from a drifting Maxwellian (flow plus thermal sampling) with sample_bkg_velocity. The Coulomb logarithm uses the Debye length and the expectation value of the impact parameter b0, and is clamped to be at least 1. The background species is assumed to be singly charged with ni = ne. An error is printed if the Coulomb logarithm or s is NaN.

Parameters:

  • bkg Background plasma, used to interpolate the flow velocity.
  • imp_time_step Time step (s).
  • T Temperature of the background species colliding with the impurity (eV).
  • mass_kg Mass of the background species (kg).
  • Te Electron temperature (eV), used for the Debye length.
  • ne Electron density (m^-3).
  • t Time of the particle (s).
  • x Computational x coordinate of the particle.
  • y Computational y coordinate of the particle.
  • z Computational z coordinate of the particle.
  • vX Cartesian X velocity of the impurity (m/s).
  • vY Cartesian Y velocity of the impurity (m/s).
  • vZ Cartesian Z velocity of the impurity (m/s).
  • q Charge state of the impurity. Must not be 0.
  • slots Particle slots, used for the impurity mass.
  • rng Random number generator for this thread.

Returns:

{s, gX, gY, gZ}, where gX, gY and gZ are the Cartesian components of the relative velocity (m/s).

docs.title: function nanbu_coll
docs.text:
void Collisions::nanbu_coll (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    bool elec,
    const double dt,
    Impurity::Statistics & imp_stats,
    std::vector< pcg32 > & rngs
)

Updates the Cartesian velocity of every particle due to Coulomb collisions with one background species using the Nanbu model.

Dead and neutral particles are skipped. For each particle, ne and Te (and Ti for ions) are interpolated at the particle location, then s, A and chi are calculated and the velocity is updated with nanbu_post_coll. Since this happens after the Boris update, the updated velocity is v at n+1/2. An error is printed if ne < 0 or chi is NaN.

For ion collisions, s * weight * dt is also added to imp_stats so the average s in each cell can be calculated later.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots. The velocities are updated in place.
  • bkg Background plasma.
  • opts Simulation options, used for the background masses (gkyl_elec_mass_amu, gkyl_ion_mass_amu) and min_ti.
  • elec If true, collide with electrons (Te). Otherwise collide with ions (Ti, limited to at least min_ti).
  • dt Time step (s).
  • imp_stats Impurity statistics, where the s values are summed for ion collisions.
  • rngs Random number generators, one per OpenMP thread.

docs.title: function nanbu_coll_kernel
docs.text:
void Collisions::nanbu_coll_kernel (
    Slots::SlotsDevice slots_d,
    const Background::BackgroundDevice bkg_d,
    bool elec,
    const double dt,
    ImpurityStats::StatisticsDevice stats_d,
    pcg32 * rngs_d,
    const double elec_mass_amu,
    const double ion_mass_amu,
    const Options::OptionsDevice * opts_d
)

Kernel that updates the Cartesian velocity of each particle due to Coulomb collisions with one background species using the Nanbu model.

One thread handles one slot, and dead particles are skipped. ne, Te (and Ti for ions) are interpolated at the particle location and held at or above min_ne, min_te and min_ti. Then s, A and chi are calculated and the velocity is updated with nanbu_post_coll_cuda. Since this happens after the Boris update, the updated velocity is v at n+1/2. A message is printed if chi is NaN.

Parameters:

  • slots_d Particle slots on the device. The velocities are updated in place.
  • bkg_d Background plasma on the device.
  • elec If true, collide with electrons (Te). Otherwise collide with ions (Ti).
  • dt Time step (s).
  • stats_d Impurity statistics on the device. Currently unused, since recording s is commented out.
  • rngs_d Random number generators on the device, one per slot.
  • elec_mass_amu Electron mass (amu).
  • ion_mass_amu Main ion mass (amu).
  • opts_d Simulation options on the device, used for min_ne, min_te and min_ti.

Calculates the post-collision Cartesian velocity of the impurity in the Nanbu collision model (Eq. 20a).

  • vZ Cartesian Z velocity of the impurity before the collision (m/s).
  • rng Random number generator for this thread.

Returns:

Post-collision velocity {vX, vY, vZ} in Cartesian space (m/s).

docs.title: function calc_bkg_flow
docs.text:
void Gkyl::calc_bkg_flow (
    grid_data_t & grid_data,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_uz,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_uX,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_uY,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_uZ,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_bX,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_bY,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_bZ,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_eX,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_eY,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_eZ,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_dbdX,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_dbdY,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_dbdZ,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_viperp_sq,
    const Options::Options & opts
)

Calculates the Cartesian components of the background ion flow.

The flow is the projection of the parallel-to-z flow onto the magnetic field direction, plus the ExB drift, E x B / B^2, plus the grad-B drift, (m v_perp^2 / (2 q B^3)) B x grad(B). The ions are assumed to be singly charged.

Parameters:

  • grid_data Tuple of the time and grid vectors (see read_gkyl).
  • gkyl_uz Ion flow parallel to z (m/s).
  • gkyl_uX Array the X component of the flow (m/s) is stored in.
  • gkyl_uY Array the Y component of the flow (m/s) is stored in.
  • gkyl_uZ Array the Z component of the flow (m/s) is stored in.
  • gkyl_bX Magnetic field X component (T).
  • gkyl_bY Magnetic field Y component (T).
  • gkyl_bZ Magnetic field Z component (T).
  • gkyl_eX Electric field X component (V/m).
  • gkyl_eY Electric field Y component (V/m).
  • gkyl_eZ Electric field Z component (V/m).
  • gkyl_dbdX X component of grad(B) (T/m).
  • gkyl_dbdY Y component of grad(B) (T/m).
  • gkyl_dbdZ Z component of grad(B) (T/m).
  • gkyl_viperp_sq Ion perpendicular thermal velocity squared (m^2/s^2).
  • opts Simulation options, used for the ion mass.

docs.text:
template<typename T>
void Gkyl::calc_gradients (
    grid_data_t & grid_data,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_vp,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_eX,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_eY,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_eZ,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_emag,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_bmag,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_dbdX,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_dbdY,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_dbdZ,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dxdX,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dxdY,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dxdZ,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dydX,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dydY,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dydZ,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dzdX,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dzdY,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dzdZ,
    const Options::Options & opts
)

Calculates the electric field and the magnetic field gradient in Cartesian coordinates.

The gradients of the potential and the magnetic field magnitude are first calculated in computational coordinates with central differences (forward or backward differences at the edges), assuming a uniform grid. They are then converted to Cartesian components using the reciprocal basis vectors (Eq. 2.6.35 in D'haeseleer), with E = -grad(Vp). The basis vectors are taken from the first time slice.

Template parameters:

  • T Floating-point type of the basis vectors.

Parameters:

  • grid_data Tuple of the time and grid vectors (see read_gkyl).
  • gkyl_vp Plasma potential (V).
  • gkyl_eX Array the electric field X component (V/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_eY Array the electric field Y component (V/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_eZ Array the electric field Z component (V/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_emag Array the electric field magnitude (V/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_bmag Magnetic field magnitude (T).
  • gkyl_dbdX Array the X component of grad(B) (T/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_dbdY Array the Y component of grad(B) (T/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_dbdZ Array the Z component of grad(B) (T/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_dxdX Reciprocal basis vector component dx/dX.
  • gkyl_dxdY Reciprocal basis vector component dx/dY.
  • gkyl_dxdZ Reciprocal basis vector component dx/dZ.
  • gkyl_dydX Reciprocal basis vector component dy/dX.
  • gkyl_dydY Reciprocal basis vector component dy/dY.
  • gkyl_dydZ Reciprocal basis vector component dy/dZ.
  • gkyl_dzdX Reciprocal basis vector component dz/dX.
  • gkyl_dzdY Reciprocal basis vector component dz/dY.
  • gkyl_dzdZ Reciprocal basis vector component dz/dZ.
  • opts Simulation options.

void Gkyl::check_tdim (
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_arr,
    const Options::Options & opts
)

Checks that the number of frames in the loaded background matches that requested for the simulation, printing an error if not.

This only needs to be run once. It is useful if the user is reusing an already calculated background, but changed the frames in the input file. In that case the background files should be deleted so that they can be regenerated, since the default is to read any existing files. Note you can circumvent this error checking if the range of frames stays the same, but that's a fringe case and not worth the effort to protect against at the moment.

Parameters:

  • gkyl_arr Any loaded array with dimensions (t, x, y, z).
  • opts Simulation options, used for gkyl_frame_start and gkyl_frame_end.

    grid_data_t & grid_data,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & ecomp
)

Applies a fix to the y boundaries of gradient-calculated data, where the gradient generally messes up due to not as many points around.

The y boundaries are treated as periodic, and the first and last cells in y are replaced with weighted averages of the second and second to last cells. This is generally a hack, since it is not clear what to do in this situation. Ideally, the gradient calculation would handle this, but I haven't been able to figure it out. Currently unused.

Reads in a Gkeyll dataset using a python interface to postgkyl, read_gkyl.py.

Species-specific data (density, temperature, par_flow and vperp_sq) is saved to bkg_from_pgkyl_[species]_[data_type].bin, and everything else to bkg_from_pgkyl_[data_type].bin. If that file already exists it is loaded directly, unless force_load is true. Otherwise read_gkyl.py is called to create it. The magnetic field and geometry files don't include the DG interpolation settings, so for those the settings saved when an earlier dataset was loaded are passed to read_gkyl.py.

Either way, the times, grid edges and cell centers in grid_data are also loaded.

docs.title: function read_gkyl
docs.text:
Background::Background Gkyl::read_gkyl (
    const Options::Options & opts
)

Entry point for reading Gkeyll data into Flan.

Each needed dataset is loaded from the Gkeyll case, either by calling read_gkyl.py through postgkyl or, if they already exist, from the files it saved on a previous run. The electric field and magnetic field gradient are then calculated, along with the background flow if the moments are BiMaxwellian. Finally every array is moved (not copied) into a Background object.

Time-dependent data is 4D with dimensions (t, x, y, z). Time- independent data (the Jacobian, metric coefficients, basis vectors and covariant components of the magnetic field) is read in as 4D, and a single time slice is stored as 3D (x, y, z). In both cases the arrays are indexed according to the Gkeyll computational coordinate indices.

This file uses the convention that all variable names are lowercase, except x,y,z always refers to computational (Gkeyll, curvilinear) coordinates and X,Y,Z always refers to physical (Cartesian) coordinates.

Parameters:

  • opts Simulation options.

Returns:

Background object holding the Gkeyll data.

docs.title: function read_magnetic_field
docs.text:
template<typename T>
void Gkyl::read_magnetic_field (
    grid_data_t & grid_data,
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_bX,
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_bY,
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_bZ,
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_bR,
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_bmag,
    const Options::Options & opts
)

Reads in the magnetic field and calculates its Cartesian components.

Gkeyll provides the Cartesian components of the magnetic field unit vector and the magnitude. The unit vector is not guaranteed to have a magnitude of 1.0 at the cell centers, so each one is renormalized to 1.0 and then multiplied by the magnitude. The number of unit vectors with a magnitude outside [0.95, 1.05] is printed. bR is the magnitude of the X-Y components.

docs.title: function record_stats_cpu
docs.text:
void Impurity::record_stats_cpu (
    Statistics & imp_stats,
    const Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    const double dt
)

Records the statistics of every alive particle into its cell and time frame.

For each particle, the count is incremented and weight * dt (the occupancy, in number of particles) is added to the weights. The velocities and charge are added multiplied by weight * dt, so they can later be turned into weighted averages.

Every thread writes straight into the shared arrays with atomic updates. In my basic testing this approach is much faster than the buffered approach (commented out above), though it's possible the buffered approach wins ground when there are significantly more particles than grid cells. That's because in that case particles may be fighting over accumulating stats in a cell, which can get held up in the atomics here. I am partial to the atomic approach just because it's so much cleaner.

Parameters:

  • imp_stats Statistics to record into.
  • slots Particle slots.
  • opts Simulation options. Currently unused.
  • dt Time step (s).

docs.title: function calc_density
docs.text:
void Impurity::Statistics::calc_density (
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const int tot_imp_num,
    const double imp_source_scale_fact=1.0
)

Calculates the impurity density in each cell and time frame from the weights.

The weights were accumulated as weight * dt, so they are already in number of particles, and the particle weights were normalized by the number of particles when each particle was created. The density is then just the weight divided by the cell volume in physical space, J * dx * dy * dz. The density array is allocated here.

Parameters:

  • bkg Background plasma, used for the grid and Jacobian.
  • tot_imp_num Total number of impurities followed. Currently unused.
  • imp_source_scale_fact Number of particles/s a single particle represents. Currently unused.

bool ImpurityTransport::all_dead_wrapper (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    Slots::SlotsDevice & slots_d,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    int rem_parts
)

Checks whether the simulation is finished, choosing the CPU or GPU implementation.

The simulation is finished when no particles are waiting to be launched and every particle in slots is dead. If rem_parts is positive, false is returned without checking slots. If GPU acceleration is on (use_gpu), Slots::all_dead_gpu is called, which copies data from the GPU and so implicitly synchronizes it. The GPU branch only exists in CUDA builds.

Parameters:

  • slots Host-side particle slots (used on the CPU path).
  • slots_d Device-side particle slots (used on the GPU path).
  • opts Simulation options, used to check whether the GPU is on.
  • rem_parts Number of particles still waiting to be launched.

Returns:

True if no particles remain to be launched and every slot is dead, false otherwise.

Applies Coulomb collisions with the background ions and electrons to every particle in slots (CPU implementation).

Particle velocities are updated in place with the Nanbu collision model. Collisions with the background ions are always applied. docs.title: function find_containing_cell_cpu
docs.text:
void ImpurityTransport::find_containing_cell_cpu (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg
)

Finds the background time index and spatial cell indices for every particle in slots (CPU implementation).

Time and space are handled differently. The background times are stored at "time centers" rather than on a grid, so the time index is the index of the background time nearest to the particle's time. The spatial coordinates are defined by grid edges, so each spatial index is the index of the cell that contains the particle's x, y and z coordinates. Particles outside the grid are assigned the first or last cell in that dimension.

The indices are written back into slots with set_tidx, set_xidx, set_yidx and set_zidx. The loop over particles is parallelized with OpenMP. Every slot is updated, including slots holding dead particles.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots whose positions are read and whose time and cell indices are updated.
  • bkg Background plasma that provides the time array and the x, y and z grid edges.

docs.title: function follow_impurities
docs.text:
Impurity::Statistics ImpurityTransport::follow_impurities (
    Background::Background & bkg,
    Options::Options & opts,
    Timer::Timer & timer
)

Follows every impurity particle through the background plasma and returns the accumulated statistics.

This is the top-level driver for impurity transport. It sets up the impurity statistics arrays, loads the OpenADAS rate coefficients (one MPI rank at a time, to avoid every rank reading the same files at once) and allocates the particle slots, with min(slot_cap, imp_num) slots. All slots start dead so the first fill launches particles into them.

On GPUs, the data is copied to each GPU, a random number generator is set up for each GPU thread, and gpu_worker runs main_loop on every GPU concurrently. The statistics and timers from each GPU are then combined and the device memory is freed. On CPUs, one random number generator is created per OpenMP thread and main_loop is called directly. If GPU acceleration was requested in a build without CUDA, it is turned off.

If the seed option is negative, random number generators are seeded from the clock so each run is different. Otherwise the seed option is used. In both cases the MPI rank is added to the seed so each rank gets a different sequence.

Parameters:

  • bkg Background plasma to follow the particles through.
  • opts Simulation options. use_gpu may be turned off if Flan was built without GPU support.
  • timer Timer that accumulates the time spent in each step.

Returns:

Impurity statistics accumulated from every particle followed on this rank.

void ImpurityTransport::main_loop (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    Slots::SlotsDevice & slots_d,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const Background::BackgroundDevice & bkg_d,
    Impurity::Statistics & imp_stats,
    ImpurityStats::StatisticsDevice & imp_stats_d,
    const OpenADAS::OpenADAS & oa_ioniz,
    const OpenADAS::OpenADASDevice & oa_ioniz_d,
    const OpenADAS::OpenADAS & oa_recomb,
    const OpenADAS::OpenADASDevice & oa_recomb_d,
    Options::Options & opts,
    Options::OptionsDevice * opts_d,
    Timer::Timer & timer,
    int & ioniz_warnings,
    int & recomb_warnings,
    const OpenADAS::IonizRecombWarningsDevice & warnings_d,
    std::vector< pcg32 > & rngs,
    pcg32 * rngs_d,
    int & max_time_ctr
)

Runs the main particle-following loop until every particle has been launched and followed until it dies.

The imp_num particles are split evenly between the MPI ranks, with the remainder going to the last rank. When running on GPUs, each rank's share is split again between its GPUs, with the remainder going to device 0. The slots are then filled, and the starting velocities are pushed back half a time step as the Boris algorithm requires. Each iteration of the loop then:

  • Updates charge states from ionization/recombination (if imp_iz_recomb is on).
  • Applies collisions (if imp_collisions is on).
  • Updates velocities with the Boris algorithm.
  • Advances particle positions.
  • Checks the time and spatial bounds.
  • Replaces dead particles with new ones.
  • Finds the containing cell of each particle.
  • Records statistics.

Each step is timed with a scoped timer. Progress is printed by rank 0 and GPU device 0 only.

Parameters:

  • slots Host-side particle slots.
  • slots_d Device-side particle slots (GPU only).
  • bkg Host-side background plasma.
  • bkg_d Device-side background plasma (GPU only).
  • imp_stats Host-side impurity statistics.
  • imp_stats_d Device-side impurity statistics (GPU only).
  • oa_ioniz Host-side OpenADAS ionization rate coefficients.
  • oa_ioniz_d Device-side OpenADAS ionization rate coefficients (GPU only).
  • oa_recomb Host-side OpenADAS recombination rate coefficients.
  • oa_recomb_d Device-side OpenADAS recombination rate coefficients (GPU only).
  • opts Simulation options.
  • opts_d Device-side simulation options (GPU only).
  • timer Timer that accumulates the time spent in each step.
  • ioniz_warnings Counter of particles whose ionization probability exceeded 1.
  • recomb_warnings Counter of particles whose recombination probability exceeded 1.
  • warnings_d Device-side warning counters (GPU only). On the GPU path, ioniz_warnings and recomb_warnings are not updated here; the counts are read back at the end of the run.
  • rngs Host-side random number generators, one per OpenMP thread (CPU only).
  • rngs_d Device-side random number generators (GPU only).
  • max_time_ctr Counter of particles that exceeded the maximum allowed time.

docs.title: function step_cpu
docs.text:
void ImpurityTransport::step_cpu (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    const double dt,
    int & max_time_ctr
)

Advances every alive particle in slots by one time step (CPU implementation).

Each alive particle's time since launch (pt) and background time (t) are increased by dt, and its x, y and z positions are advanced using its current velocity. If the particle's time since launch exceeds the imp_max_time option, the particle is marked dead and max_time_ctr is incremented. The iteration counter of each stepped particle is also incremented. Dead particles are skipped. The loop over particles is parallelized with OpenMP.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots to advance.
  • bkg Background plasma (currently unused).
  • opts Simulation options, used for imp_max_time.
  • dt Time step (s).
  • max_time_ctr Counter of particles that exceeded the maximum allowed time. Incremented atomically.

std::pair< double, double > OpenADAS::calc_ioniz_recomb_probs (
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const OpenADAS & oa_ioniz,
    const OpenADAS & oa_recomb,
    const double dt,
    const double t,
    const double x,
    const double y,
    const double z,
    const double q,
    const double Z
)

Calculates the probabilities that a particle ionizes or recombines during one time step.

ne and Te are interpolated at the particle location, and each probability is rate * ne * dt. A fully ionized particle can't ionize and a neutral can't recombine, so those probabilities are 0.

Parameters:

  • bkg Background plasma.
  • oa_ioniz OpenADAS ionization (scd) rate coefficients.
  • oa_recomb OpenADAS recombination (acd) rate coefficients.
  • dt Time step (s).
  • t Time of the particle (s).
  • x Computational x coordinate of the particle.
  • y Computational y coordinate of the particle.
  • z Computational z coordinate of the particle.
  • q Charge state of the particle.
  • Z Atomic number of the impurity.

Returns:

{ionization probability, recombination probability}. Either can be greater than 1 if the time step is too large.

void OpenADAS::ioniz_recomb (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const OpenADAS & oa_ioniz,
    const OpenADAS & oa_recomb,
    const double dt,
    int & ioniz_warnings,
    int & recomb_warnings,
    std::vector< pcg32 > & rngs
)

Updates the charge state of every particle due to ionization and recombination.

For each particle, a random number is drawn for each process and the process occurs if it is less than its probability from calc_ioniz_recomb_probs. If both occur they cancel out and the charge is unchanged. Probabilities greater than 1 mean a smaller time step should be used if they happen often, so they are counted in ioniz_warnings and recomb_warnings.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots. The charges are updated in place.
  • bkg Background plasma.
  • oa_ioniz OpenADAS ionization (scd) rate coefficients.
  • oa_recomb OpenADAS recombination (acd) rate coefficients.
  • dt Time step (s).
  • ioniz_warnings Incremented by the number of particles with an ionization probability greater than 1.
  • recomb_warnings Incremented by the number of particles with a recombination probability greater than 1.
  • rngs Random number generators, one per OpenMP thread.

std::string OpenADAS::OpenADAS::get_openadas_path (
    const std::string_view openadas_root,
    const int openadas_year,
    const int imp_atom_num,
    const std::string_view rate_type
)

Assembles the full path to an OpenADAS data file, e.g., [openadas_root]/scd50/scd50_w.dat.

An error is printed if rate_type is not "scd" or "acd", or if there is no OpenADAS data for imp_atom_num. Supported elements are H through Ne, Al, Si, Cl, Ar, Fe, Kr, Mo, Xe and W.

Parameters:

  • openadas_root Full path to the directory containing the OpenADAS data.
  • openadas_year Year of the OpenADAS data to load, e.g., 50.
  • imp_atom_num Atomic number of the impurity to load data for.
  • rate_type Either "scd" (ionization) or "acd" (recombination).

Returns:

Full path to the OpenADAS file.

docs.title: function get_rate_coeff
docs.text:
double OpenADAS::OpenADAS::get_rate_coeff (
    const int charge,
    double ne,
    double te
) const

Returns the rate coefficient for a charge state, bilinearly interpolated in Te and ne.

ne and Te outside the range of the OpenADAS data are clamped to the minimum or maximum value, so the rates are never extrapolated.

Parameters:

  • charge Index of the rate coefficient table. For ionization this is the charge, and for recombination the charge - 1.
  • ne Electron density (m^-3).
  • te Electron temperature (eV).

Returns:

Rate coefficient (m^3/s).

docs.title: function read_rate_coefficients
docs.text:
void OpenADAS::OpenADAS::read_rate_coefficients (
    std::ifstream & openadas_stream
)

Reads in the header, densities, temperatures and rate coefficients from an OpenADAS file, storing them in the class.

The densities and temperatures are stored in the file as log10(ne [cm^-3]) and log10(Te [eV]), and the rate coefficients as log10(rate [cm^3/s]). They are converted to ne (m^-3), Te (eV) and rate (m^3/s). The rates are stored with dimensions (charge, Te, ne). An error is printed if there are fewer than two densities or temperatures, since the bilinear interpolation needs at least two of each.

Parameters:

  • openadas_stream Open file stream of the OpenADAS file.

docs.title: function crosscheck_options
docs.text:
void Options::crosscheck_options (
    Options & opts
)

Checks that the options are compatible with each other, changing them if needed.

Currently this only checks that Nanbu collisions are used with BiMaxwellian moments from Gkeyll. If not, a warning is printed and collisions are turned off. Placeholders are left for checks of particle splitting and the variable time step.

Parameters:

  • opts Options object to check and modify in place.

docs.title: function load_input
docs.text:
void Options::load_input (
    Options & opts,
    const Inputs & inpts
)

Loads each input option into an Options object, overwriting the default value.

Each option name is matched to its setter in Options and the value is set with assign_option. An error is printed for an option name that is not recognized, or a value of the wrong type, and that option is left unchanged.

Parameters:

  • opts Options object to load the options into. Generally should be passed in right after constructing it.
  • inpts Input options assembled in a simulation's input file.

docs.title: function load_options
docs.text:
Options Options::load_options (
    const Inputs & inpts
)

Creates an Options object from the input options.

Starts from an Options object with the default values, then overwrites them with any options given in inpts. Finally the options are checked to be compatible with each other with crosscheck_options, which may change some of them.

Parameters:

  • inpts Input options assembled in a simulation's input file.

Returns:

Options object with the values from inpts. Options that are not in inpts keep their default values.

docs.title: function initialize_control_ints
docs.text:
void Options::Options::initialize_control_ints ()

Sets every control integer to match its string option.

Control integers are integer versions of string options that are faster to check in the code than comparing strings. The logic that assigns each one lives in the option's setter, so this calls every such setter with the option's current value. Any new option with a control integer must have its setter called here too. Otherwise its control integer stays at -1, which get_control_int reports as an error.

docs.title: function fill_slots_cpu
docs.text:
void Slots::fill_slots_cpu (
    Slots & slots,
    int & rem_parts,
    int & alive_slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    std::vector< pcg32 > & rngs
)

Replaces dead particles with new ones, as long as there are particles remaining to be followed.

The dead slots are counted first. The number refilled is the smaller of the dead count and rem_parts, and rem_parts is reduced by that number. Each refilled slot gets a new particle from make_new_particle, using the random number generator of the thread doing the work, with its particle time reset to 0 and its state set to alive.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots to refill.
  • rem_parts Number of particles still to be followed. Reduced by the number of particles created, and never goes below 0.
  • alive_slots Set to the number of alive slots after refilling.
  • bkg Background plasma.
  • opts Simulation options.
  • rngs Random number generators, one per OpenMP thread.
